title: A celebrity cluster in the spotlight
caption: The galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+2223, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: MACS J1149.5+2223 · constellation Leo · about 5 billion light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, C. Willott (National Research Council Canada), R. Tripodi (INAF - Astronomical Observatory of Rome)

recognition.text: Ranked #27 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Large blue spirals, pale white ellipticals and many orange and red galaxies fill this deep Webb view. This is the galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+2223, about 5 billion light-years away in Leo. More than 300 member galaxies have been confirmed, with several hundred more possible, and a huddle of ghostly ellipticals rules its center.

The cluster's gravity bends light from galaxies behind it, an effect called gravitational lensing, stretching some into narrow streaks and twisting others into strange shapes. Just below the bright central galaxies, a spiral galaxy has been drawn out into something resembling a pink jellyfish. That galaxy hosts a star that once held the record as the farthest single star known, plus a supernova that showed up as four separate images simultaneously.
MACS J1149 was one of six clusters in Hubble's Frontier Fields program, chosen because their strong lensing lets astronomers see into the early universe.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.40 x 2.41 arcminutes) and distance (5 billion light years), the frame spans roughly 3.5 million × 3.5 million light-years. Its light set out about 5,000 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light, with the shortest filters shown in blue, middle ones in green and the longest in red.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye.

explore: Webb is now reaching even earlier times, turning up discoveries such as a supermassive black hole feeding heavily under 600 million years after the Big Bang. These data come from the CANUCS program #1208, which studies low-mass galaxies in the early universe and the epoch of reionization, when the earliest stars and galaxies began to shine.
alt: Many galaxies on a black background, including large blue spirals, pale white ellipticals, and numerous orange and red galaxies down to tiny faint spots.
